batchName: Early Rome & the Kingdom: The Foundation of an Empire (753-509 BCE) - Easy Batch 3
chapterName: Early Rome & the Kingdom: The Foundation of an Empire (753-509 BCE)

questions.question: Which port at the mouth of the Tiber was founded by King Ancus Marcius?
questions.explanation: Ancus Marcius founded Ostia at the river's mouth. He also settled conquered Latins on the Aventine Hill, forming the origins of the plebeians.
questions.sourceQuote: He founded Ostia, a port at the river's mouth, and settled conquered Latins on the Aventine Hill, forming the origins of the plebeians, Rome's common people.

questions.question: According to the traditional story, whose crime against the noblewoman Lucretia set off the uprising against Rome's last king?
questions.explanation: The king's son Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia. She told her husband and father, then killed herself, and her death sparked the uprising.
questions.sourceQuote: According to the traditional story, the crisis came when the king's son Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, a virtuous noblewoman.

questions.question: Who wrote the first history of Rome, around 200 BC?
questions.explanation: Fabius Pictor wrote the first history of Rome around 200 BC, about three centuries after the kings fell. Later writers such as Livy relied largely on oral tradition.
questions.sourceQuote: The first history of Rome was written by Fabius Pictor around 200 BC, about three centuries after the kings fell.

questions.question: According to the story, how did the war that followed the seizure of the Sabine women end?
options: Romulus killed the Sabine king in single combat
The Etruscans forced both sides to make peace
A storm scattered the two armies
The women threw themselves between the armies
questions.explanation: The captured women stopped the fighting by throwing themselves between the armies. Afterwards the Romans and Sabines united into one people.
questions.sourceQuote: It ended only when the captured women threw themselves between the armies.

questions.question: What replaced the king as Rome's leadership after the revolt?
options: A single dictator chosen for life
questions.explanation: Rome began electing two consuls every year instead of a king. The first two were Brutus and Collatinus, Lucretia's husband.
questions.sourceQuote: In place of a king, Rome now elected two consuls each year, starting with Brutus and Collatinus.

questions.question: According to tradition, who led the revolt against Tarquin the Proud?
questions.explanation: The revolt was led by Lucius Junius Brutus, the king's own nephew. Tradition dates it to 509 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: It was led by Lucius Junius Brutus, the king's nephew.

questions.question: According to legend, which god fathered Romulus and Remus?
questions.explanation: The twins were said to be sons of Mars, the god of war. Their mother, Rhea Silvia, had been forced to become a Vestal Virgin, a priestess sworn to chastity.
questions.sourceQuote: She nevertheless bore twins, Romulus and Remus, supposedly fathered by Mars, the god of war.

questions.question: According to tradition, Rome's fifth king, Tarquinius Priscus, was an immigrant born into which people?
questions.explanation: Tarquinius Priscus was traditionally born an Etruscan, one of the wealthy peoples living north of Rome in what is now Tuscany. He became Rome's first Etruscan king.
questions.sourceQuote: According to tradition he was born an Etruscan, one of the wealthy, powerful peoples living north of Rome in what is now Tuscany.

questions.question: In the legend, which animal suckled the abandoned twins Romulus and Remus?
questions.explanation: A she-wolf suckled the twins in a cave called the Lupercal. A shepherd named Faustulus then raised them.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead a she-wolf suckled them in a cave called the Lupercal, and a shepherd named Faustulus raised them.

questions.question: Which writer's poem "Lucrece" was inspired by the story of Lucretia?
questions.explanation: Lucretia's story inspired Shakespeare's poem Lucrece. It also inspired many paintings in the 18th and 19th centuries.
questions.sourceQuote: The tale later inspired Shakespeare's poem Lucrece and many paintings in the 18th and 19th centuries.
